new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the lexical root (roots are iambic CVC / CVCV́C); prefixes, infixes and most suffixes are unstressed, so surface position varies with morphology (root-final = word-final in unsuffixed words, penultimate or earlier when unstressed suffixes follow). Braine treats primary stress as phonemically marked but almost fully predictable from morpheme class; grammatical words (pronouns, particles) may lack inherent stress, in which case the macrosegment gets default stress on its first syllable. Whitehead 1925 gives compatible surface tendencies (disyllables final unless penult long; accent on the stem rather than affixes).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Braine 1970 p.34-35: primary stress has allophones [ˊ] primary, [ˋ] secondary, [ˇ] tertiary distributed within the macrosegment (tertiary between primary stresses, full primary macrosegment-finally); no word-level rhythmic secondary stress rule stated. Braine p.173-174: CVC suffix syllables following a stressed root tend also to bear stress (e.g. stressed allomorph of {hat}).
new_statements.exceptions: Long vowels nearly always co-occur with stress but a few unstressed function words have long vowels (ʔinre· 'and', po·ʔ 'because', ye· 'if') (Braine p.64); some suffixes ({hat}, {ŋac}, {perih}) have stressed allomorphs; Whitehead notes disyllables with initial accent (yih'-tör, ta'-rik, pi'-sik) and occasional final long-syllable accent in polysyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Braine's unit for stress allophony and default placement is the macrosegment (intonational phrase); word-level primary stress is a property of (root) morphemes. Sidwell's statement is explicitly about the phonological word. Pitch (four levels) is intonational, not lexical (Braine p.29).
new_statements.identity_note: All three quoted sources describe Car Nicobarese proper (Pū, island of Car Nicobar; Glottolog carn1240, ISO caq). Braine's data are from a single Car speaker recorded in the 1960s (Munda Languages Project, Chicago/Berkeley). Temple 1903's stress remark (on file) concerns Central Nicobarese (Nancowry, cent1990) and was used only as context.

sources.citation: Whitehead, George. 1925. Dictionary of the Car-Nicobarese Language. Rangoon: American Baptist Mission Press ('Notes on the Car-Nicobarese language', front matter).
sources.note: p. xxvi: 'Tentative rules as to the Accent... In dissyllables the accent is generally on the final syllable, unless the penultimate syllable is long; yet we say yih'-tör, ta'-rik, pi'-sik. In trisyllables and polysyllables the accent is generally on the penultimate or antepenultimate, according as either of these is long. If both are short, it is generally on the antepenultimate... but it sometimes falls on a final long syllable... Naturally the accent generally falls on the stem, rather than on prefixes or suffixes.'

sources.citation: Sidwell, Paul. 2018. Proto-Nicobarese phonology. In H. Ring & F. Rau (eds.), Papers from the Seventh International Conference on Austroasiatic Linguistics (JSEALS Special Publication 3), 101-131. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press.
sources.note: p.105 sec.2.1.1 (Car word/syllable structure): 'Words consist of lexical roots, which can be one- or two-syllable iambs (the rightmost syllable of lexical roots bears the primary word stress), plus various prefixes, infixes, and suffixes.' Full vowel inventory only in stressed (root-final) syllables; unstressed syllables restricted to 3-4 nuclei; length and nasalization contrastive only in stressed nuclei. Synthesis of Braine 1963/1970 and Whitehead 1925.
